Summary:

This manuscript addresses an important and interesting question: in spite of a wealth of information available on NTPases it is still largely unclear how these enzymes are activated. These proteins constitute a large fraction of cellular enzymes and play a number of key roles in mechano-chemical events. Hence understanding molecular mechanisms of their activation, in particular by monovalent cations, is fundamental for our understanding of many important biological processes.

Shalaeva et al. describe the results of detailed molecular dynamics (MD) simulation analyses of solvated Mg-ATP in the presence and absence of potassium, sodium or ammonium ion, and compare the data with that observed in Mg-ATP/GTP bound to various P-loop NTPases. The major conclusion is that potassium and ammonium ions interact with the α and γ oxygens of the nucleoside to stabilize Mg-ATP in an extended conformation similar to that observed in P-Loop NTPases. Sodium was found to be too small to simultaneously interact with the α and γ oxygen atoms of a protein-bound extended phosphate chain. These observations help explain why some P-loop NTPases can be activated only by potassium and not sodium.

Overall, the work is detailed and the analysis rigorous; it is presented clearly and logically. Reviewers appreciated the attention to detail as well as the extensive citations accompanying a very useful Introduction and thoughtful Discussion. The comparative analysis of the role of Lys/Arg residues (such as from GAP proteins or another domain) with those of potassium and sodium is instructive.

We found that the manuscript lacks a couple of important pieces of information, and may benefit from some clarifications.

Essential revisions:

1) The major question deals with the objective difficulties in distinguishing monovalent cations from water molecules in crystal structures, due to a rather similar number of electrons and very weak anomalous signals produced by Na+ and K+. And although Na+ could in principle be distinguished owing to shorter coordinating distances, coordinating distances for the potassium ion are a perfect match to hydrogen bonding with molecules of water. Owing to this, reliable assignments can be made only on the basis of high resolution crystallographic structures (<1.8Å or so) and even then it would be advisable further validating such assignments through careful inspection of crystallographic data. In this regard, was resolution of crystals structures taken into account when selecting PDB entries for analysis and have crystal data been validated? Also, considering the availability of a large number of structures for NTPases, we wonder if there are cases where high resolution structures have been determined for both K+ and Na+ complexes? And if so, how these data (after appropriate validation) compare with the results of MD simulations presented in this paper?

2) The other issue involves MD simulation of Mg-ATP bound to NTPases. Despite the useful comparison of the MD data in solution conducted on the isolated Mg-ATP with the protein-bound nucleoside in X-ray structures, the two are clearly in very different conditions and therefore conclusions drawn from the comparative analysis are somewhat indirect. In addition, as the authors discuss in multiple places including the subsection “Activation of P-loop NTPases by monovalent cations”, crystallization conditions prevented observation of the ion or the K-loop entirely, thus making comparison difficult. This can be remedied by conducting MD on nucleoside-NPTase complexes; for at least one or two systems. This can be done reasonably easily. For example, at least in RAS GTPases, metal ions from bulk solvent readily bind to the phosphate group during MD simulations (e.g., https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28498561).

3) The third concern is that all of the simulations were conducted on ATP while most of the protein structure analysis involved GTPases. It appears that the underlying assumption is that ATPases and GTPases are mechanistically the same or at least similar. This may well be the case, and appears to be the subject of a separate article, but it would be helpful to the reader if the authors provided evidence to this effect. For example, conducting a few simulations of Mg-GTP in the presence of sodium and potassium should be straightforward.

4) Throughout the manuscript both "extended" and "eclipsed" conformations of the nucleoside are described as hydrolysis prone, although the latter is probably more prone. It would be helpful to somehow make a distinction.

5) Based on their work and some previous reports, such as the article cited above, it would seem that the nucleotide binding site of P-loop NTPases is susceptible to binding to monovalent metal ions, at least in the absence of compensatory interactions such as with GAPs. This raises the question as to whether a certain fraction of all NTPases may exist in a monovalent metal bound form in the cell. Authors' comment on this issue would be valuable.

6) Final, and somewhat minor, concern is a "diluted" end of the paper (Discussion section). We would encourage authors to add a clear set of brief conclusions at the very end, summarizing their findings and views on the role of monovalent cations and Arg/Lys fingers in the catalysis and the rationale for choosing one particular option for activation.

7) Avoid referring to the second "submitted" paper (Shalaeva et al.), because this paper remains unpublished and you wished to consider its submission separately.

results.result: MD simulations of Mg-NTP complexes in water with K+, Na+, and NH4+ ions revealed that these monovalent cations bind to two distinct sites on the phosphate chain: the BG site (between β- and γ-phosphates) and the AG site (between α- and γ-phosphates). The coordination bond distances were 2.2 Å for Na+, 2.6 Å for K+, and 2.7 Å for NH4+, consistent with crystallographic data. The BG site showed higher occupancy than the AG site for all cations tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C31-C35 are well-supported by MD simulation data presented in Figures 2 and supplementary materials. The identification of two binding sites (BG and AG) is clearly demonstrated, and the coordination bond distances are validated against crystallographic data (C32). The occupancy measurements (C35) are quantified and shown in Figure 2C-E.

results.result: The extended conformation of the NTP phosphate chain, similar to that observed in P-loop NTPase crystal structures, was achieved in water only with K+ and NH4+ ions, but not with Na+ ions. Na+ ions induced contracted or curled conformations with shorter PA-PG distances, while K+ and NH4+ ions produced extended conformations that matched the catalytically-prone conformations in enzyme active sites, including transition state-like conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C39-C42, C52-C53, C56-C58 are strongly supported by MD simulation data and comparison with crystal structures shown in Figures 4, 5, and Table 1. The heat maps in Figure 5 clearly demonstrate the differential effects of cations on phosphate chain conformation, with K+ and NH4+ producing extended conformations that overlap with enzyme-bound NTP conformations, while Na+ produces contracted conformations.

results.result: Binding of a second K+ ion in the AG site stabilized the phosphate chain in a near-eclipsed conformation, with the α-phosphate bonds almost coplanar to β- and γ-phosphate bonds. This transition was energetically favorable, with binding of the second K+ ion promoting the eclipsed conformation by approximately 27 meV (2.5 kJ/mol).
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by MD simulation data with positional restraints shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1D. The energetic calculation (C37) is presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, providing quantitative support for the stabilization effect.

results.result: MD simulations of the K+-dependent GTPase MnmE demonstrated that binding of the activating K+ ion between α- and γ-phosphates led to rotation of the γ-phosphate group, yielding an almost eclipsed, catalytically productive conformation. The K+ ion shortened the O2A-O3G distance from 5.3 Å to 4.7 Å and twisted the γ-phosphate to form a new H-bond with Asn226. The rotation primarily affected the γ-phosphate (Ψα-γ changed from ~66° to 38°) while α- and β-phosphate angles remained relatively stable.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C74-C84, C88 are well-supported by MD simulation data of MnmE GTPase shown in Figure 7 and supplementary figures. The structural changes are quantified with specific angle measurements and distance changes. The formation of the new H-bond with Asn226 (C75-C76, C84) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7A-B.

results.result: The binding sites for monovalent cations observed in MD simulations of Mg-NTP complexes in water exactly matched the positions occupied by positively charged groups in crystal structures of P-loop NTPases. The BG site is always occupied by the conserved P-loop lysine, while the AG site is occupied by either K+/Na+ ions or Arg/Lys fingers. K+ and NH4+ ions in water produced extended phosphate chain conformations similar to those in enzyme active sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C98-C100 are strongly supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 6, which demonstrates the correspondence between MD simulation-derived cation binding sites and crystal structure positions. This is a key finding linking the solution behavior to enzyme mechanisms.

results.result: In all analyzed crystal structures of diverse P-loop NTPases, the conserved P-loop motif maintains the triphosphate chain in an extended, catalytically prone conformation through numerous interactions with phosphate groups. This extended conformation is similar to that imposed on NTPs in water by K+ or NH4+ ions, but not Na+ ions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47, C60, C87, C156 are supported by extensive structural analysis of P-loop NTPases presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 5-7. The conservation of the extended conformation across diverse P-loop NTPase families is well-documented, and the comparison with MD simulation data (Figures 5-6) validates the similarity to K+/NH4+-induced conformations.

results.result: Activation of K+-dependent NTPases requires specific interaction of the P-loop domain with activating partners (proteins, domains, or RNA/DNA) to shape the functional cation-binding site. Structural analysis of MnmE and Era showed that the K-loop is disordered in inactive states but becomes stabilized and competent for K+ binding upon interaction with activating partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C69, C138-C139, C144, C146 are supported by comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2-3. The contrast between inactive and active conformations of MnmE and Era clearly demonstrates the requirement for activating partner interaction to form functional K+-binding sites.

results.result: The mechanism requiring specific interaction with activating partners prevents uncontrolled hydrolysis of cellular NTP stocks. M+-dependent NTPases are almost inactive in isolation and only become active after binding to activating partners, which is essential to prevent cell death from NTP depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C172-C173, C178 are supported by logical inference from the structural and functional data. The requirement for activating partner interaction (C29, C144) combined with the poor intrinsic K+ binding to the AG site (C130, C174) provides a mechanistic explanation for controlled activation. This is further supported by the observation that very high K+ concentrations (>>100 mM) are needed for activation in the absence of physiological partners (C175).

results.result: Analysis of 17 crystal structures of cation-dependent P-loop NTPases revealed PA-PG distances of 4.9-5.3 Å for non-hydrolyzable analogs and 5.3-5.6 Å for transition state analogs, similar to MD simulation results with K+ ions. Surprisingly, very few structures of K+-dependent GTPases contained K+ ions in their AG sites, and K-loops were often unresolved or distorted.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by structural analysis presented in Table 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The PA-PG distance measurements (C62) are quantified in Table 3, and the comparison with MD simulation data (C63) validates the computational approach. The observation about missing K+ ions and disordered K-loops (C64-C65) is documented in supplementary materials.

results.result: Dynamins represent a unique case of Na+-adapted P-loop NTPases. While Na+ ions produce contracted phosphate chains in MD simulations, dynamin crystal structures show extended conformations even with Na+ bound. This adaptation required at least three mutations: replacement of conserved Asn with Ser in the P-loop, shortening of the K-loop by one residue, and replacement of the K-loop Asn with Glu. These changes allow the K-loop to stabilize Na+ in the AG site through alternative interactions, with the free O2A atom coordinated by the backbone amide of the shortened K-loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C199 are well-supported by structural analysis and comparison between dynamins and K+-dependent NTPases shown in Figures 1C, 8, and cited literature (Ash et al., 2012; Chappie et al., 2010). The specific mutations (C189-C191) are identified through structural comparison, and their functional consequences (C192-C196) are explained through structural analysis. The requirement for multiple mutations (C199) explains the rarity of Na+ adaptation.

results.result: The extended phosphate chain conformation typical of Mg-NTP complexes in the presence of large monovalent cations (K+, NH4+) is more prone to hydrolysis than the compressed conformation observed with Na+. This suggests that the P-loop could have been shaped in K+- and/or NH4+-rich, but Na+-limited environments. Na+ binds most tightly to the phosphate chain, producing contracted/curled conformations, while K+ and NH4+ form longer coordination bonds resulting in wider angles and longer PA-PG distances, but bind more weakly.
results.evaluation: Claims C111, C158-C164 are supported by MD simulation data (Figures 4-5, Table 1) and comparison with crystal structures. The inference about evolutionary implications (C159) is speculative but logically follows from the data. The binding affinity differences (C160, C163) are documented in Supplementary file 1B and Figure 2C-E.

results.result: Binding of K+ in the AG site brings the phosphate chain into an almost eclipsed conformation in both Mg-ATP in water and MnmE GTPase. In enzyme-bound NTPs, rotation of α-phosphate is prevented by multiple interactions, but the γ-phosphate can rotate due to its position as an end group. The network of bonds around γ-phosphate (H-bonding with conserved Lys, backbone amides, and Mg2+ coordination) is flexible enough to permit pronounced rotation into an almost eclipsed position, where repulsion by α- and β-phosphate oxygen atoms promotes hydrolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C113, C117-C121 are supported by MD simulation data (Figures 3, 7) and structural analysis. The mechanism is well-explained through the combination of computational and structural data. The inference about γ-phosphate flexibility (C118-C120) is supported by structural considerations and the observed rotation in MD simulations.

results.result: The rotation of the γ-phosphate group induced by K+ binding could represent the basic mechanism of hydrolysis by P-loop NTPases. The shape of the P-loop and pattern of NTP binding are extremely well conserved across all P-loop NTPases, suggesting that activating entities could rotate γ-phosphate and promote stabilizing H-bonds in other P-loop NTPase families.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C129 represent speculative conclusions extrapolating from the MnmE data to all P-loop NTPases. While the conservation of the P-loop is well-documented (C129, supported by Figure 6), the claim that γ-phosphate rotation represents the 'basic mechanism' for all P-loop NTPases (C89) is not directly tested. The manuscript acknowledges this is speculative ('could represent'). Additional experimental validation across diverse P-loop NTPase families would be needed to fully support this generalization.

results.result: P-loop NTPases represent the most common protein fold (up to 18% of gene products), apparently predating the Last Universal Cellular Ancestor. The P-loop fold is a 3-layer αβα sandwich with the characteristic Walker A motif (GxxxxGK[ST]) forming the P-loop. The conserved lysine forms H-bonds with β- and γ-phosphates, while the Ser/Thr coordinates Mg2+. P-loop NTPases are typically activated by Arg or Lys 'fingers' inserted upon interaction with activating partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10, C85 describe well-established background knowledge about P-loop NTPases, supported by extensive citations to published literature. These claims provide the foundation for the study and are not contested. The structural features (C3-C6) are illustrated in Figure 1.

results.result: Two competing mechanistic proposals exist for P-loop NTPase activation: Gerwert and colleagues proposed that the Arg finger rotates α-phosphate toward an eclipsed conformation favoring bond cleavage through oxygen repulsion, while Blackburn and colleagues proposed that Arg insertion reshuffles the H-bond network to position the attacking water molecule.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 accurately describe prior mechanistic proposals from the literature, supported by appropriate citations (Rudack et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2016; Gerwert et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2016, 2017a, 2017b). These provide context for the current study's findings.

results.result: Some apparently ancestral P-loop NTPases are activated by K+ ions rather than Arg/Lys fingers. K+-dependence has been shown for numerous proteins including MnmE, Era, YqeH, FeoB, and translation factors. The catalytic K+ ion occupies the position of the Arg/Lys finger and requires a specific K-loop and Asn/Asp residues in the P-loop. Na+ cannot replace K+ in most cases. The existence of K+-dependent NTPases and K+-dependent translation requires maintaining high cytoplasmic [K+]/[Na+] ratios, which can consume up to half of cellular energy.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22, C86 are well-supported by extensive citations to published literature documenting K+-dependent NTPases and their properties. The structural features (C18-C19) are supported by cited crystallographic studies (Scrima and Wittinghofer, 2006; Ash et al., 2012; Anand et al., 2010) and illustrated in Figure 1B.

results.result: Human dynamin and A. thaliana dynamin-like protein are equally well activated by Na+ and K+ ions, with Na+ binding in a similar position to K+ in other NTPases. Historically, larger ions (K+, Rb+) were shown to be more efficient than smaller ions (Na+, Li+) in accelerating transphosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by appropriate citations (Chappie et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2011; Ash et al., 2012; Lowenstein, 1960). These observations motivate the investigation of cation size effects in the current study.

results.result: Bond cleavage between β- and γ-phosphates proceeds via a planar transition complex with widening of the PB-O3B-PG angle. Binding in P-loop NTPase active sites constrains the Mg-NTP complex to particular conformations that are catalytically prone, increasing hydrolysis rates by several orders of magnitude even without activating moieties. MD simulations showed that without M+ ions, the phosphate chain was remarkably elongated with large PA-PG distances not observed in crystal structures or with added cations. Only transition state analogs with severely widened angles (>135°) were not matched by MD conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C38, C48-C51, C54-C55, C59 are supported by citations to established literature (C38, C49) and MD simulation data compared with crystal structures (Figures 4-5). These observations characterize the conformational space of NTPs and provide context for understanding cation effects.

results.result: During catalytic turnover, two MnmE proteins undergo conformational changes allowing dimerization of their G-domains for mutual activation. In crystallized full-length MnmE dimers, K-loops are unresolved and no K+ binding is observed. In isolated G-domain dimers with transition state analogs, K-loops and cations are resolved. Dimerization requires both GTP and K+ ions; Na+ cannot support dimerization. In Era-rRNA complexes crystallized without K+, the K-loop attains the proper shape with a complete cation-binding site occupied by water.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68, C140-C143 are supported by structural analysis of MnmE and Era (Figure 6—figure supplements 2-3) and citations to published studies (Meyer et al., 2009; Böhme et al., 2010; Tu et al., 2011). These observations demonstrate the conformational changes required for K+ binding and activation.

results.result: In K+-dependent GTPase Era crystallized without K+, the potential K+ binding site contains a water molecule 2.9-3.4 Å from six ligands. In RecA-like recombinase RadA, two K+ binding sites exist: one roughly corresponding to the AG site (shifted toward γ-phosphate) and another between γ-phosphate and catalytic Glu (corresponding to the G-site from MD simulations). In RecA-like recombinases, the K+ ion is coordinated by a conserved Asp from an adjacent monomer, differing from TRAFAC NTPases but similarly requiring activating partner interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C147-C150 are supported by structural analysis of Era (PDB: 3R9W) and RadA (PDB: 3EW9) shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 3-4, with appropriate citations (Tu et al., 2011; Li et al., 2009; Qian et al., 2006). These examples illustrate variations in K+-binding mechanisms across different P-loop NTPase families.

results.result: NTP hydrolysis releases large amounts of free energy from phosphate group repulsion, but the cumulative negative charge repels attacking nucleophiles, securing stability without NTPases. Previous computational studies used model systems (methyl triphosphate, Mg-ATP, Mg-GTP) but contained no monovalent cations. Current mechanistic views posit that the γ-phosphorus is attacked by a hydroxyl from a pre-polarized water molecule, requiring several positive charges to compensate negative charges. P-loop NTPases use at least four positive charges: Mg2+, conserved P-loop Lys, and either an activating M+ ion or Lys/Arg residue.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97 accurately describe established knowledge about NTP hydrolysis mechanisms and previous computational approaches, supported by appropriate citations. The identification of the gap in previous computational studies (C93) motivates the inclusion of monovalent cations in the current work.

results.result: In enzyme active sites, the extended NTP conformation is maintained by interactions with P-loop side chains and backbone atoms. In MnmE GTPase, specific H-bonds and coordination bonds fix the phosphate chain in extended conformation. Stabilization in extended conformation dramatically increases hydrolysis rates even without activating moieties (e.g., 5 orders of magnitude in Ras-like GTPases). In bound NTPs, β- and γ-phosphates are in an eclipsed state due to Mg2+ and Lys interactions, causing repulsion that could explain higher hydrolysis rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C110 are supported by structural analysis (Figures 1B, 7, Table 1) and citations to published literature (Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011; Kötting and Gerwert, 2004; Shutes and Der, 2006; Delbaere et al., 2004; Matte et al., 1998). These observations characterize the enzyme-bound state and provide mechanistic context.

results.result: Insertion of activating moieties accelerates hydrolysis by additional orders of magnitude. In enzyme-bound NTPs, α-phosphate rotation is prevented by interactions of the entire NTP molecule with the enzyme. In MnmE, α-phosphate forms a stable H-bond with the backbone amide that persists even in inactive states. The moieties on both sides of α-phosphate are tightly fixed, impeding rotation around PA bridging bonds, especially when the P-loop domain interacts with its activator.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C114-C116 are supported by citations (Wittinghofer, 2006; Kamerlin et al., 2013) and MD simulation data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The structural constraints on α-phosphate rotation are well-documented through MD simulations and structural analysis.

results.result: The H-bond between O2G and the backbone nitrogen of Asn226 is seen in most P-loop NTPase structures with NDP-AlF4- (transition state analog) but rarely with non-hydrolyzable analogs, suggesting it contributes to transition state stabilization. In most P-loop NTPases, the Asn226 counterpart is a small residue (Gly/Ala), indicating backbone flexibility. In K+-dependent NTPases, this position has Asn/Asp coordinating the activating cation. The activating cation interacts directly with O3G and indirectly with O2G via the Asn/Asp backbone nitrogen. Formation of these bonds would reshuffle the H-bond network around γ-phosphate, important for catalysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C128 are supported by structural analysis across P-loop NTPase families (Figures 1B, 6, 7) and reference to Shalaeva et al., 2018. The differential presence of the O2G-Asn226 H-bond in transition state vs. non-hydrolyzable analogs (C122-C123) supports its role in catalysis. The inference about functional relevance (C124, C127-C128) is reasonable based on the structural data and citations to mechanistic literature.

results.result: The affinity of the AG site for K+ is intrinsically low, requiring a full-fledged K-loop (extended Switch I region) to provide additional ligands. The absence of K+ from most crystal structures could be due to absence from crystallization medium, difficulty distinguishing K+ from water by electron density (at 60% occupancy they are indistinguishable), or incomplete M+-binding sites when K-loops are unresolved or distant from active sites. Additional factors beyond sequence features affect K+ binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 are supported by MD simulation data (Supplementary file 1B, Figure 2C), structural analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A), and citations to relevant literature (Ash et al., 2012; Kuhle and Ficner, 2014; Shui et al., 1998). The explanations for missing K+ in crystal structures are reasonable and well-supported.

results.result: Proper K-loop conformation is crucial for cation binding as it provides two backbone oxygen ligands. P-loop NTPases emerged before bacterial-archaeal divergence. Lupas and colleagues hypothesized the ancestor was an NTP-binding protein incapable of fast hydrolysis. The P-loop was identified as an antecedent domain segment and a 'nest' for phosphate groups. Milner-White proposed that first catalytic motifs were short glycine-rich sequences. The P-loop may have been shaped by high K+/NH4+ levels in early cellular habitats. The match between P-loop shape and large cations is consistent with suggestions of life emerging in terrestrial K+- and nitrogen-rich environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C145, C151-C155, C165-C169 describe evolutionary context and hypotheses, supported by appropriate citations (Lupas et al., 2001; Leipe et al., 2002; Alva et al., 2015; Bianchi et al., 2012; Watson and Milner-White, 2002; Torrance et al., 2009; Mulkidjanian et al., 2012; Dibrova et al., 2015). The evolutionary speculation (C167-C169) is consistent with the data showing K+/NH4+ produce extended conformations matching enzyme-bound NTPs.

results.result: The conformational space of Mg-NTP in water reflects preferred conformations with monovalent cations. Activating Arg/Lys residues are provided by interactions with other domains, monomers, proteins, or DNA/RNA, allowing tight control. For TRAFAC cation-dependent NTPases, the K-loop is part of the same domain. Poor K+ binding to the naked AG site manifests in the need for very high K+ concentrations (>>100 mM) for activation without physiological partners. The functional K-loop is distorted in inactive states but attains functional shape upon activator interaction. In eIF5B structures with non-physiological crystal-packing contacts forming quasi-K-loops, GTP molecules remain (indicating no hydrolysis) and PA-PG distances are shorter than in active conformations. Additional factors beyond cation binding may control catalysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C157, C170-C171, C174-C177, C179-C182 are supported by MD simulation data, structural analysis (Table 2, Figure 6—figure supplements 1-3), and citations (Fasano et al., 1982; Kuhle and Ficner, 2014; Shalaeva et al., 2018). The observations about eIF5B (C179-C181) demonstrate the specificity required for functional activation.

results.result: The low probability of the specific combination of mutations required for Na+ adaptation may explain why only dynamins show this adaptation. Arg/Lys residues are widespread as P-loop NTPase activators. In some cases (e.g., TRAFAC NTPases), it was possible to trace how Arg residues replaced K+ ions evolutionarily. Recruiting Arg/Lys as activating moieties is relatively simple and makes catalysis independent of cellular K+/Na+ level oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C203 are supported by the structural analysis of dynamin adaptations (C188-C199), data in Table 2, and citations (Mulkidjanian et al., 2012; Dibrova et al., 2015; Shalaeva et al., 2018). The inference about evolutionary replacement (C202-C203) is reasonable given the widespread distribution of Arg/Lys-activated NTPases.

results.result: Although Na+ cannot activate most P-loop NTPases, its binding may be physiologically relevant. Gorfe and colleagues observed tight Na+ binding to GTP phosphates in Ras GTPases (activated by Arg fingers, not K+), suggesting Na+ might prevent Tyr32 H-bonding with γ-phosphate or hinder Arg/Lys finger access. In active cells, cytoplasm contains much more K+ than Na+, so K+ binding to AG sites of K+-independent NTPases is weak and unlikely to hinder activators. However, in energy-limited prokaryotic cells, [K+]/[Na+] ratios reverse. Dormant cells retain NTP stocks for awakening. High Na+ in dormant cells could suppress metabolism by blocking both K+-dependent and K+-independent NTPases.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C215 present speculative hypotheses about Na+ roles in cellular regulation. While the observations from Gorfe and colleagues are properly cited (C205, Alva and Lupas, 2018; C207, Sayyed-Ahmad et al., 2017), and the cellular K+/Na+ dynamics are documented (C209, C211-C213), the proposed mechanism for NTP stock retention in dormant cells (C214-C215) is speculative. The suggestion that Na+ could hamper K+-independent NTPases (C215) extrapolates beyond the direct evidence. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring experimental validation.

results.result: The tridentate αβγ-coordination is found in K+-dependent chaperonin GroEL and related proteins. GroEL and Mm-cpn were inhibited by Na+ even when added over K+. In GroEL structures, K+ was identified in the AG site position with PA-PG distances (4.3-4.4 Å) similar to MD simulations of tridentate Mg-ATP with K+ (4.32 ± 0.24 Å). K+ increases nucleotide affinity in GroEL. The phosphate chain retains flexibility in GroEL-type ATPases, with shape depending on cation size. Na+ binding would produce contracted, less catalytically prone conformations. Na+ added over K+ would inhibit ATP hydrolysis due to tighter binding. This example shows that balancing negative charge compensation with maintaining catalytically-prone conformations may be important for other NTPase superfamilies beyond P-loop NTPases.
results.evaluation: Claims C216-C227 are supported by structural analysis (PDB: 1PQC, 1KP8, 3RUV, 3RUW) and citations (Kusmierczyk and Martin, 2003; Chaudhry et al., 2003; Wang and Boisvert, 2003; Pereira et al., 2012; Grason et al., 2008). The comparison with MD simulation data (C220) validates the computational approach for different coordination modes. The inference about broader applicability (C226-C227) is reasonable but speculative.
